六孔橫笛常見於管笛鼓樂隊、軍隊與行進樂隊，也用於民間音樂，尤其凱爾特音樂。加勒比: The fife is common in fife-and-drum bands, in the army and in marching bands, and is also used in folk music, especially Celtic music. Caribbean music more often uses bamboo fifes; Appalachian folk music uses the fife for lively dance tunes, and the American slave tradition developed fife-and-drum blues. In Europe it appears in Languedoc and Nice in southern France, in Basel in Switzerland, and where the Lambeg drum accompanies it in Northern Ireland. It is also used at the Junkanoo festivals of the Bahamas and Jamaica, and in the bamboo fife music of northeast Brazil.
六孔橫笛為小型高音橫向氣鳴樂器，靠吹口孔吹氣發聲，音色尖銳明亮，接近短笛。傳統六: The fife is a small, high-pitched transverse aerophone sounded by blowing across the blowhole; its timbre is sharp and bright, close to the piccolo's. The traditional six-hole instrument uses diatonic fingerings and in practice is mostly used in D, G and A major and their relative minors, with some semitones out of tune; modern ten- or eleven-hole versions can play semitones. A skilled player gets three octaves, and marching bands mostly use the second and third octaves, because the high register is the loudest and carries best, which is what suits military and drum bands playing outdoors.
六孔橫笛為橫向氣鳴樂器，演奏時橫持管身，以氣流橫吹吹口孔發聲。六孔版以雙手食指、: The fife is a transverse aerophone: hold the body sideways and direct the air across the blowhole. The six-hole version uses the index, middle and ring fingers of both hands; the modern ten-hole version keeps the same finger positions and adds the thumbs and little fingers for the chromatic notes, and the eleven-hole version adds a hole below the right middle finger. A beginner should learn the diatonic fingerings and the second and third octaves first, since the six-hole instrument has few notes available and the third-octave fingerings are harder.
六孔橫笛的管身主要以木料製成，如黑木、格瑞那迪拉、玫瑰木、莫帕尼木、粉紅象牙木、: The body of the fife is mainly wood, such as blackwood, grenadilla, rosewood, mopane, pink ivory, cocobolo, boxwood, maple and persimmon; some are made entirely of metal or plastic. Military and marching instruments often have metal rings protecting both ends, and where use is gentler a turned knob-shaped ornament may protect the end instead. Modern versions may be in two or three pieces and may have a metal or cork sliding tuning joint. Some bamboo fifes from the Caribbean and Brazil belong to the same class.
六孔橫笛（Fife）是一種小型、高音調的橫吹氣鳴樂器，近似短笛，Hornbost: The fife is a small, high-pitched transverse aerophone similar to the piccolo, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.121.12. Traditional instruments are mostly tuned diatonically, with six fingerholes and one blowhole in the body, and sound when air is blown across the blowhole; modern chromatic types have ten or eleven fingerholes and can play any note. It originated in medieval Europe and is commonly used in fife-and-drum bands, military bands and marching bands.
管笛起源於中世紀歐洲，英文名稱源自德語中表示管子的詞彙。早期為六孔全音階橫吹氣鳴: The fife originated in medieval Europe, and its English name comes from the German word for a pipe. Early instruments were six-hole diatonic transverse aerophones, and modern versions have developed into ten- or eleven-hole chromatic ones. From the fifteenth century Swiss and south German armies used soldier's pipes, which came to western Europe with mercenary troops and by the sixteenth century had become the standard instrument of European infantry; in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries it was tied to the signalling system of infantry companies, with two fifers and two drummers to a company and the rank of fife major appearing. It later entered the fife-and-drum traditions of the Celtic lands, Appalachia, southern France, Basel in Switzerland, Northern Ireland and the United States.
